isTeamAdminOrOwner is built with isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...), so only a team owner passes this check - team admins who aren't owners are rejected, although the name and intent say admin or owner

When the request uses a different email casing, the filter fails to recognize an existing attendee and compares the input against an already-lowercased blacklist case-sensitively, inserting duplicate attendee identities and permitting blacklisted variants

When email delivery fails, the catch discards the exception after the attendee and calendar updates have completed, so the mutation reports success without a retryable record and newly added guests receive no invitation

When guests contains an address already present on the booking, sendAddGuestsEmails receives it as a new guest even though uniqueGuests excluded it from the insert, sending that existing attendee AttendeeScheduledEmail as if they were newly added
When the input contains the same new address more than once, uniqueGuests retains every occurrence because it only compares against existing attendees, so createMany inserts duplicate Attendee rows

When the dialog is dismissed with Escape or a backdrop click, AddGuestsDialog only updates isOpenDialog, so multiEmailValue and isInvalidEmail remain mounted in the parent and reappear on the next open, allowing stale addresses to be submitted

When utils.viewer.bookings.invalidate() is still pending or rejects, the onSuccess callback closes the dialog and reports success without waiting for the booking list refresh, so the visible list can remain stale and a refresh failure becomes an unhandled rejection

Attendees are persisted before the calendar update and email with no recovery - prisma.booking.update commits the new attendees first, and if eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees throws, the mutation returns an error but guests are already stored, causing retry to hit uniqueGuests.length === 0 branch with misleading BAD_REQUEST

When any non-SMS workflow reminder has retryCount > 1, the deleteMany removes it because the retry branch is not constrained by method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, so email or WhatsApp reminders can be lost when the SMS cron runs

When two concurrent handler invocations read the same unscheduled reminder, both call twilio.scheduleSMS before these updates, so each schedules a duplicate Twilio message and both writes use the same prior retryCount, leaving the counter one increment behind and preventing deletion after two failures

When twilio.scheduleSMS succeeds but the preceding scheduled: true update fails transiently, the catch path increments retryCount while leaving the reminder unscheduled, causing duplicate SMS on next cron run

When a reminder has no rendered message or no sendTo, the guard before twilio.scheduleSMS skips both the retry branch and the catch, leaving it unscheduled with the same retryCount and processing it on every cron run indefinitely
When a reminder row is written with a negative retry count, the scheduler's retryCount > 1 cleanup condition never removes it and subsequent failures can keep it below the retry threshold
Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can throw if prisma.workflowReminder.update fails, aborting the cron loop and leaving remaining reminders unprocessed

When a caller constructs InsightsBookingService with scope: "team" but omits teamId, InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions accepts it, safeParse fails, and buildAuthorizationConditions returns NOTHING_CONDITION, so the request silently receives no bookings instead of team-scoped results. When fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache finishes a refresh, updateManyByCredentialId passes an empty update object, so Prisma does not have a field update to execute and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt remains unchanged; the connected-calendar cache status therefore continues to show the previous refresh time. When a delegated credential or a connection-modification-disabled view is used, canDisconnect only hides the menu item, while viewer.credentials.delete still accepts the credential ID and handleDeleteCredential performs no matching restriction check. Resolve the .env path from the script location (or require an explicit repository root), because relative paths are interpreted using the caller's working directory. Running ./scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh from the repository root targets ../.env outside the repository, while running it from scripts/ targets a different file, so the app may not receive the webhook URL and an unintended .env can be created.

The script uses the BSD/macOS sed -i '' form, but the repository's shell tooling also uses GNU-compatible sed -i and this script has no platform guard. On Linux, GNU sed treats the empty argument as a file and errors instead of replacing the variable, so the script prints success only after a failed update and the webhook URL remains unchanged.

Do not identify/reuse a tunnel solely by this broad process match and a shared log path. pgrep -f can return multiple or unrelated matching PIDs, and the log can be stale or belong to another concurrent invocation; in that case extract_url_from_log may configure a URL unrelated to the process being reused (or reuse a tunnel that has already exited).

The error paths call cleanup, but cleanup always exits with status 0. Therefore a rate-limit hit or failure to extract a tunnel URL reports an error while the script still succeeds to callers, so automation can continue with an unset/invalid GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Preserve a nonzero status for failure paths (while keeping an intentional interrupt/normal shutdown successful).

Authorization failure thrown as plain Error instead of TRPCError. When a user passes a credentialId they don't own, deleteCacheHandler throws a bare Error. tRPC maps it to INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (500), which is logged as a server fault and hides the real cause. Throw new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN" }) or NOT_FOUND instead.

dev:cron uses npx tsx but tsx is not declared as a dependency. When a developer runs yarn dev:cron, npx tsx downloads tsx on the fly, because the script no longer uses the declared ts-node. The script then runs an unpinned, undeclared tool and fails offline or in CI sandboxes. Add tsx to devDependencies with a pinned version and call tsx cron-tester.ts.

When a workflow is deleted, the loop starts deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder without awaiting or aggregating them, so the mutation deletes the workflow and returns while the provider cancellation is still pending; in a serverless request that ends early, the scheduled email/SMS remains active and is sent

When SendGrid cancellation fails while deleting a workflow, deleteScheduledEmailReminder logs the error and returns without marking the reminder cancelled, then the workflow deletion cascades away the workflowReminder row, so the cron job has no record to retry and the scheduled email can still be sent

When twilio.cancelSMS fails for a reminder from a disabled event type, deleteScheduledSMSReminder catches the error and leaves the provider schedule and workflowReminder row unchanged, so the SMS is still sent and no later job retries it because the cancellation cron only selects cancelled reminders for email cancellation

When a workflow step is edited, forEach(async ...) starts deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder without awaiting or aggregating them, so the mutation can return before the cancellation is persisted or sent to the provider
When the database update fails, deleteScheduledEmailReminder catches and only logs the error, so the SendGrid scheduled email remains active and is sent for the cancelled booking
When twilio.cancelSMS fails, deleteScheduledSMSReminder only logs the error and leaves the reminder row intact, but unlike email reminders there is no SMS cron path that retries rows left behind
immediateDelete path still uses the SendGrid cancel call that fails once 100 cancellations are pending, sets no cancelled flag and has no retry

When requestReschedule returns or its serverless invocation is terminated before the floating promises finish, the reminder cancellation is not persisted, so the previous booking's workflow email or SMS can still be sent

When a booking is cancelled, handler returns without awaiting deleteScheduledEmailReminder or deleteScheduledSMSReminder, so the provider cancellation request can still be in flight when the request/serverless invocation ends
When rescheduling, the async cancellation is invoked without await, so eventManager.reschedule and the response path can proceed while the SendGrid cancellation is still in flight

When a reschedule has an email reminder with a reference ID, deleteScheduledEmailReminder takes the immediate path and returns after cancelling SendGrid without deleting or marking the workflowReminder row, leaving stale workflow data
When immediateDelete is used while rescheduling a booking, the branch cancels SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder row behind with cancelled unset

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch - when client.request throws for one reminder, the for loop exits into the single outer catch and every later reminder in remindersToCancel is skipped

Deferred cancellation misses emails scheduled to send before the next cron run - if a booking is cancelled or rescheduled less than about 15 minutes before the reminder's scheduled time, the email may still be sent
Reminder cancellation promises are not awaited - deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async and called inside forEach without await or collection
try/catch cannot catch the async cancellation failures because deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async and unawaited, so the log.error branch is dead

When a reschedule has calendar or video references, the async callback is launched without being awaited, so the handler sends the reschedule email and continues before deleteEvent/deleteMeeting completes, while adapter failures become unhandled rejections. Await all deletions with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => ...)) or use a sequential for...of before sending the email.

When a booking has a calendar or video reference, Reschedule starts the async deletion and then sends the reschedule email without waiting for it, so the external event/meeting can remain active while the operation reports success; any rejection also bypasses this surrounding try/catch because forEach discards the callback promises. Replace forEach with an awaited Promise.all and await each deletion so failures are observed before continuing.

When a reschedule has calendar or video references, Reschedule starts each deletion in an async forEach but does not await the returned promises, so it sends the reschedule email and returns true before cleanup finishes, while any rejection bypasses this surrounding try/catch and can leave the old event or meeting active. Await a Promise.all of the reference deletions or use a sequential for...of before sending the email.

When a recurring booking is cancelled, the forEach callback yields at await getCalendar(credential), so handler reaches await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) before this callback pushes its deleteEvent promise into apiDeletes; the booking and references are then deleted while the external calendar events remain. Replace this async forEach with an awaited for...of/Promise.all collection before the database cleanup.

async forEach makes calendar/video deletions floating promises that the try/catch cannot catch - when Reschedule runs, bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) now awaits getCalendar but forEach discards the returned promises, so a rejection from getCalendar, calendar.deleteEvent or deleteMeeting bypasses the surrounding try/catch and logger.error, becoming an unhandled rejection.

requestReschedule deletes calendar events in an unawaited async forEach - when a reschedule is requested, bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) awaits getCalendar, then calls deleteEvent or deleteMeeting, and nothing awaits the result. The handler goes on to sendRequestRescheduleEmail and returns while the calendar and video deletions are still running.

When any server path imports appStore, every registry entry starts loading immediately, so an operation that needs one integration still downloads and evaluates all 28 app modules, retaining most of the startup cost this change is intended to remove. Make entries lazy (for example, memoized loader functions/getters) and update consumers to invoke only the selected loader.

Recurring-cancel deletion loop runs in an unawaited async forEach, so apiDeletes is incomplete - when a recurring booking is cancelled with allRemainingBookings, .forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) }) is not awaited. The new await getCalendar adds another suspension before the push.

appStore still loads every app eagerly, and the developer docs now describe the wrong pattern - each entry is import("./app") evaluated when the module loads. All ~28 app modules start loading on first import of @calcom/app-store, so this is not lazy loading. Every entry is a promise created at module scope, and a failed import of any app becomes an unhandled rejection even if that app is never used.

Slot inside a date override returns true and skips the busy-time check - when a slot's start date matches a date override and the slot lies inside it, checkIfIsAvailable hits if (dateOverrideExist) return true, skipping the busy.every(...) check, allowing double-bookings

Working-hours check uses the same value for start and end - end is computed from slotStartTime so it equals start, meaning slot's end time is never checked against workingHour.endTime, allowing slots that run past working hours
Working-hours check uses find which returns true when any single workingHour entry that includes the day excludes the slot, incorrectly rejecting valid slots

When a generated slot extends past a host's working-hours end, checkIfIsAvailable uses the slot start for both start and end, so end > workingHour.endTime is false for every slot that begins before closing

When a slot starts exactly at a date override's end, checkIfIsAvailable accepts it because the rejection only tests slotStartTime.isAfter(...), allowing a slot at 11:00 for a 10:00-11:00 override even though no portion of that slot is inside the override

When a host has multiple working-hour intervals on the same weekday, checkIfIsAvailable rejects a slot as soon as any interval does not contain it, rather than accepting it when one interval contains it

When one host has an override on a date but another fixed or round-robin host does not, checkIfIsAvailable evaluates the flattened dateOverrides array without filtering by the host being checked, using another user's override window

When a date override falls on a daylight-saving transition, getSlots calculates the organizer offset from the synthetic UTC instant in override.start, not from the override's intended local date and time, causing one hour shift

When a timezone conversion moves an override's end past midnight, getSlots stores both endpoints as minutes within the same day, so an override such as 23:30-00:30 becomes startTime 1410 and endTime 30 and is discarded as invalid
When an override shifts across midnight into the requested invitee day, activeOverrides has already excluded it before conversion runs because it filters the raw UTC-encoded organizer wall time

When a date override has identical start and end times, the identity comparison is always false because each dayjs(...) call creates a distinct object, so zero-length override is treated as all-day available override

When an override's invitee-local date differs from the UTC date stored in override.start, activeOverrides excludes it before offset is calculated, so recurring working hours remain available and the override is ignored

When a date override spans a DST transition, getSlots applies the offset calculated at override.start to both endpoints, so endTime is shifted using the wrong organizer or invitee offset after the transition

Override offset shift can wrap past midnight when an override's start or end plus offset crosses a day boundary, causing .hour() * 60 + .minute() to wrap to a small value making endTime less than startTime
override.timeZone is optional in TimeRange, and when undefined, .tz(undefined) falls back to a default which may be incorrect

When a worker is unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive starts its replacement immediately after process.kill() without waiting for the old child to exit, causing both workers to read the same segment before either deletion and publish duplicate span payloads

When produce_to_pipe is configured, process is a threading.Thread, so the branch does not stop it at all before _create_process_for_shards starts the replacement, causing old and new threads to flush the same Redis shard concurrently and publish duplicate segments

When the consumer is started with --flusher-processes -1, SpanFlusher receives the negative value, creates no process-map entries, and raises KeyError while assigning the first shard (process_index = 0 % -1)

When an existing caller passes produce_to_pipe as the final positional argument, the inserted flusher_processes parameter receives the callback and produce_to_pipe stays None, causing SpanFlusher to pass a callable to min() and fail during startup

When --flusher-processes is set to a negative value, SpanFlusher retains it because negative integers are truthy, then num_processes is negative and the shard loop indexes a mapping with a process index that was never created, raising KeyError

When a ProcessSpansStrategyFactory caller omits flusher_processes (the constructor default), SpanFlusher treats None as len(buffer.assigned_shards) and starts one worker per assigned shard instead of preserving the prior single-worker behavior

time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched to a no-op at the top of test_basic, causing the test to depend on timing races with the flusher thread

When a queue worker's result_processor raises, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy still marks the message offset complete in OrderedQueueWorker.run's finally, so the commit loop acknowledges the failed result and a transient processing failure is permanently skipped after restart

When result_processor raises, OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the failed Kafka offset complete, so _commit_loop commits past work that was never successfully processed and Kafka will not redeliver it after restart

When decoding or grouping_fn raises, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit marks the message complete without submitting it, so the next commit permanently acknowledges a message that was never processed

When ResultProcessor.handle_result fails, ResultProcessor.__call__ catches the exception and returns, so OrderedQueueWorker.run treats the result as successful and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy commits its offset, causing the failed uptime result to be silently lost

When Arroyo closes one partition strategy during a rebalance while another partition strategy from the same factory is still active, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close shuts down the factory-wide queue_pool, causing the remaining strategy to submit to stopped workers

When grouping_fn or queue_pool.submit raises, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit marks the message complete after only logging the exception, so the commit loop acknowledges that offset and the result is permanently skipped
Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool, so later strategies silently drop messages after rebalance

When the new mode is invoked with --max-workers 0 or a negative value, uptime_options accepts it and ResultConsumer passes it to FixedQueuePool; zero/negative values create no queues, so submit catches the resulting indexing error and marks each message complete without processing it

When FixedQueuePool.shutdown runs with queued work still pending, setting worker.shutdown = True makes each OrderedQueueWorker exit after its current item, even though Queue.shutdown(immediate=False) is intended to drain the queue, causing pending messages to remain unprocessed

When incoming messages outpace the workers, FixedQueuePool creates unbounded queues, so SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit continues accepting messages without backpressure and retains every decoded WorkItem in memory, potentially exhausting the consumer process

When _commit_loop marks offsets committed, OffsetTracker.mark_committed removes them from all_offsets but leaves every completed offset in outstanding, so a long-lived consumer retains one set entry per processed Kafka message and eventually grows without bound

When the CLI supplies a negative max_workers, FixedQueuePool is created with no queues and get_queue_for_group later fails on modulo by a negative queue count, causing SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit to catch that failure and acknowledge each result, silently dropping the entire stream

test_preserves_order_within_group still passes when same-subscription processing regresses to arbitrary order because every decoded result has the same observable fields and the test checks only the count

test_concurrent_processing_different_groups still passes when FixedQueuePool serializes all workers or assigns both groups to one active worker because it waits only for four completions and checks the final count

test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions still passes when FixedQueuePool is replaced by a serial implementation because it only waits for two calls and checks their count without observing overlapping execution

A successful federated recovery-code validation never consumes the matched code. The local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider removes the next code and persists the updated credential, but this branch only checks membership; the subsequent form flow can only remove a credential when allCodesUsed(), which is never reached for this reconstructed federated credential. Consequently the same recovery code remains valid and can be replayed indefinitely.

The federated credential is persisted with only the raw list in credentialData, but the recovery credential contract requires the serialized RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData in credentialData and RecoveryAuthnCodesSecretData in secretData; RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel reads both structured fields. Thus credential-management/authentication code that reconstructs the federated model cannot reliably consume this credential, and the getCredentials workaround rebuilds a different model without preserving its ID.

Federated recovery codes trigger a re-setup required action or a bad removal call. When the user storage validates a recovery code through isValid but does not expose the credential through getCredentials, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns empty. recoveryCodeCredentialModel then stays null, so addRequiredAction(CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES) runs after every successful login.

Returning the federated credential here makes the existing recovery-code consumers operate on a credential they cannot mutate through the SubjectCredentialManager APIs. For example, after the last code is consumed, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator calls removeStoredCredentialById with this model's ID, but UserCredentialManager.removeStoredCredentialById delegates to the local/federated credential store selected by StorageId, not to the federated CredentialInputUpdater; similarly, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider's update path remains local-only. Consequently, an exhausted federated credential is not removed or updated through those paths, leaving stale recovery state.

This reconstructs a recovery credential by treating credentialData as a raw list of original codes, but getCredentials is also the source used by the new federated read path. If deserialization fails, the exception is swallowed and the method returns no recovery credential, so callers interpret an existing federated credential as absent and may fall back to local storage or trigger setup. More importantly, createFromValues hashes every list element and can throw for malformed/non-string elements; that runtime failure is not covered by the IOException catch.

Because this branch advertises recovery codes as supported by the federated updater, the credential-delete flow will select this provider, but disableCredentialType does not remove recoveryCodes. Consequently the UI/API can report a successful removal while the federated credential remains configured. Add a recovery-code case to disableCredentialType (and expose it from getDisableableCredentialTypesStream) or avoid advertising it for deletion.
